opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to where the real uncertainty is. Building another assistant that's commercially successful is a hard problem, but it's a relatively well-defined one. You know the shape of the product: a chat box, a model behind it, and you compete on capability, cost, distribution, and user experience. There are a lot of very capable teams doing that, and the marginal value of one more is... it's not zero, but it's bounded.

What excites me more is that I don't think we've figured out the right form factor for this technology yet. If you look at history, when a new general-purpose technology shows up, the first products usually look like the old things with the new technology plugged in. The early internet looked like newspapers and catalogs put online. It took a while before you got search, social networks, and things that were truly native to the medium. I feel like chat assistants are a bit like that: a very natural first form, because language is how we talk to people, so we talk to the model like a person. But that doesn't mean it's the final form.

When I was working on agents, things like ReAct and the work on language agents, one thing that became clear to me is that the interesting part isn't just the model answering a question. It's the model interacting with an environment, taking actions over long horizons, having memory, working with tools, maybe working alongside other agents or people. Once you take that seriously, the interface question becomes wide open. Should the AI be something you talk to, or something that works in the background for days? Something that lives in your existing tools, or a new kind of environment altogether? How do humans give feedback, set goals, and trust it? None of those have obvious answers.

And I also think, in terms of what I call the "second half" of AI, the bottleneck is shifting. For a long time the game was about methods: better architectures, better training, better benchmark numbers. Now the models are strong enough that the question becomes: what are we actually using them for, how do we define the right tasks, and how do we evaluate real-world utility? Product form is deeply tied to that. The product defines the task, and the task defines what the model needs to get good at. So exploring a new product form is, in a sense, also a research question. It's about defining the problem rather than just optimizing an existing one.

So for me personally, it's about where I can create the most new information. If something works, then it opens up a new direction for many people. If it doesn't, we still learn something about what the right abstraction is. Whereas if I build a slightly better assistant, I might win some market share, but I'm not sure I've changed how people think about what AI can be. I find the second one less interesting, at least for this stage of my life.

r001.rationale: He says exploring a new product form is more exciting, even if it fails because it would still teach them something, while building a slightly better assistant would be less interesting.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the assistant form factor is already quite well understood. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Doubao — they all converge on roughly the same thing: a chat box, a model behind it, you ask, it answers. The remaining work there is mostly optimization. You make the model a bit stronger, the latency a bit lower, the distribution a bit wider. That's real work, and it's commercially very valuable, but the shape of the thing is fixed. You're competing on execution, not on imagination.

What I find more interesting is that the model's capabilities have moved much faster than the product forms around them. If you look back at ReAct or at the early agent work, the whole idea was that a language model shouldn't just be a text generator — it should be something that acts in an environment, calls tools, takes multi-step actions, learns from the feedback it gets. We now have models that are genuinely capable of that. But most products still present them as a conversation partner. There's a mismatch between what the model can do and what we let users do with it.

So when I say I want to explore a new product form, I mean trying to find the interface and the interaction pattern that actually matches what agents are now. That's a much more open question. Nobody knows the answer yet. Is it something that runs for hours on your behalf? Is it something that lives inside your existing workflow, or something that replaces the workflow? How much autonomy does a user actually want, and how do you make that legible? Those are design questions as much as technical questions, and they haven't been answered.

I also think there's a research argument. The next bottleneck for agents isn't just model intelligence, it's environments and the right tasks and feedback. A new product form is also a new environment. If you build something people genuinely use to get real things done, you learn what actually matters, what fails, where the model is still weak. Another assistant doesn't teach you much that we don't already know.

And I'll admit there's a personal element. I came from research, and the reason I moved toward product was that I felt the most important questions were no longer purely about the model. Building another assistant would feel like doing something that's already been done well by very good teams. Exploring a form that doesn't exist yet — even if it fails — is the kind of thing where if it works, it changes what people think AI is for. That's the bet that feels worth making.

r001.rationale: The candidate says exploring a new product form—even if it fails—is the bet that feels worth making, while building another assistant would repeat work already done well by other teams.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is whether AI can change how we interact with computers, rather than just make the existing interaction more efficient. An assistant is a very natural starting point: you ask a question, it gives an answer, or you give it a task and it tries to complete it. And there’s a lot of commercial value in making that work well.

But I’m curious about what comes after that. If the model becomes much more capable, should the product still be a chat window waiting for you to type something? Or could it work with you in a different way—understanding the context of what you’re doing, helping you explore something before you even know exactly what to ask?

The exciting part is that we don’t yet know what that interaction should look like. You have to discover it through building, and sometimes a product experiment reveals something that a model benchmark doesn’t: a capability people find useful, or a limitation you hadn’t understood.

So commercial success matters, but it isn’t the only thing I’d want to optimize for. I’m more interested in making something that helps us discover what a computer with intelligence can actually become.

r001.rationale: The response says exploring a new AI interaction is more interesting than optimizing only for commercial success, but it does not state that this would remain more interesting even if the exploration failed.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the interesting question is what AI makes possible that wasn’t possible before. You can build a commercially successful assistant by making an existing workflow faster or more convenient, and that’s valuable. But it doesn’t necessarily answer what a new kind of product could look like.

An assistant already gives you a frame: a user asks, and the AI helps. I’m more curious about whether that’s the right frame. If a system can take actions, work over a longer period, and learn from feedback, how should people interact with it? What would they trust it to do? Exploring a new product form lets you investigate those questions together.

Commercial success is an important signal, but I’m more motivated by discovering a new way for people to use the technology. There’s more uncertainty there, and that’s part of what makes it interesting.

r001.rationale: The response says Yao is more motivated by discovering a new product form than by commercial success, but it does not say he would find that more interesting even if the exploration failed.
